speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise, under the privilege of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Inasmuch as the motor car manufacturing industry is in a financial crisis as a result of the rapidly changing market and competition from overseas, and whereas the jobs and livelihood of thousands of Canadians are threatened by the mismanagement and incompetence of the Liberal government and, in particular, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko):
That this House condemn the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce for his failure to negotiate an equitable agreement with Chrysler to safeguard Canadian jobs and for misleading this House and the Canadian people by publicly indicating on three occasions that he had reached an agreement with Chrysler.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on what is a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, not only to the residents of the Parry Sound-Muskoka region but also to the residents of all regions of the country which depend heavily upon revenue generated from tourist activity.
For the year 1978, the total revenue generated from tourist activity involving both Canadian citizens and residents of foreign countries amounted to $11.1 billion, or 5 per cent of the country's GNP. In light of the fact that the revenue
produced from activity directly or indirectly associated with the tourist industry in this country represents such a substantial proportion of the country's GNP, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson):
That an independent department of tourism be established by the current administration to be headed by a minister solely responsible for tourist activity in this country and to be staffed by individuals presently affiliated with the branch of tourism under the existing Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, pursuant to Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Section 109 of the BNA Act and Supreme Court of Canada decisions on that section clearly state that mines and minerals, including oil and gas, belong to the provinces in which they are situated. The Government of Canada has honoured that section with respect to Quebec and Ontario resources such as asbestos, lead, zinc, nickel, electricity, etc. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor):
That this House instruct the Prime Minister to recognize his personal and public duty to honour and uphold the constitution and that he instruct the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to honour section 109 in the present energy negotiations.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR DEBATE AND AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODEMOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43, to move a motion of urgent and heartrending necessity.
In view of the fact that the lives of over 60,000 innocent Canadian children were terminated by the decision of therapeutic abortion committees during the past year, and recognizing that unborn infants are not nondescript appendages attached to their mother's womb but, in fact, are living human beings to whom society has an undeniable moral responsibility, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor):
That the government be directed to convene a full parliamentary debate on this important subject at the earliest possible hour, with a view to amending the Criminal Code so as to recognize the full legal and human rights of unborn children and that, further, the three political parties represented here do consent to a free-conscience vote on the consequent amendments to the Criminal Code of Canada.

Whereas some provinces have repeatedly refused to endorse the patriation of the Constitution of Canada from Britain, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp):
That the Parliament of Canada submit an address to Her Majesty the Queen, that Her Majesty may graciously be pleased to cause a bill to be laid before the Parliament of the United Kingdom to provide for the amendment in Canada of the Constitution of Canada.

speechtext:
Before we begin the oral question period, I should like to draw the attention of the House to the presence in our gallery of our Canadian diplomats in Iran who helped in the escape of the American diplomats.

It is always satisfying when one is called upon to render service to others. I am sure that is sufficient reward to our diplomats from Iran, but I know this House would want to pay homage to the intelligence and courage of Ambassador Ken Taylor and his colleagues for having done something which makes Canada extremely proud.

speechtext: I have the honour to inform the House that I have just received a joint resolution from the Senate, and the House of Representatives of the state of Tennessee, expressing appreciation to the government and the people of Canada for the action of their diplomats in Iran. I am sure that hon. members will want me to reply on their behalf.

subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF DIPLOMATS WHO EVACUATED AMERICANS FROM IRAN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there was clearly a reversal. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce stated his intention to make an announcement at three o'clock, and a short while later he came out of the cabinet meeting and said that he was sorry, that no decision had been taken and there would be no announcement.
My question relates more to the position of the United States government. Today, the U.S. loan board will be making a decision on their aid package to Chrysler. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce indicated quite clearly that there is a very close relationship between the position the Government of Canada would take and the position of the U.S. loan board.
Because of the importance of this decision, I am sure the Prime Minister is very current on these negotiations. Could he advise whether there was something that the U.S. loan board were requesting from Canada, in their proposal, that caused this reversal to take place? Was there something that was unacceptable on the part of the U.S. loan board that caused this action?

subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF DIPLOMATS WHO EVACUATED AMERICANS FROM IRAN
speechtext:
No, Madam Speaker. The fact that the loan board was meeting today was the reason the minister had hoped to make his announcement yesterday. I repeat, discussions in cabinet indicated that we were not ready to make that decision, in spite of the meeting of the loan board today.
The minister had been attempting to reach his counterpart-I believe it is Secretary Miller-who sits on the loan board, but he was away in Yugoslavia to attend President Tito's funeral. This made it difficult for us to obtain certain
May 9, 1980

additional facts, on the one hand; on the other hand, we were informed that the government of Ontario was hoping to improve upon the package that had been discussed between Chrysler and Canadian officials and ministers.
I personally spoke to the Premier of Ontario who, indeed, confirmed to me that he hoped to improve on the package and that he was hoping to have a meeting early next week with Chrysler officials, which presumably would also be attended by the federal minister. At that time they will attempt to improve the package for Canadians. But the general desire of the federal government is still, of course, to help this industry and the workers whose jobs depend on its survival; but, of course, we bend to the superior wisdom of the Ontario government, who feel that a better deal can be reached, and we are willing to go along with that.

It was unclear to us why he was taking this rather defensive position. It occurred to me that possibly there is no contingency plan in place.
I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether there is a contingency plan in place in the event that agreement is not reached with Chrysler Canada, and in view of the very difficult position that the workers and the company and the suppliers have been put in. If there is no contingency plan in place, would he commit to the House that steps will be taken immediately to commence work on such a plan?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PETROLEUM PRICING AND AUDITING AGENCY
ESTABLISHMENT OF PETROLEUM PRICING AND AUDITING AGENCY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, my question is for the Prime Minister. During the election campaign the Liberal party promised to establish a petroleum pricing and auditing agency, one of whose functions would be to advise the government about an appropriate price for oil. I just want to remind the Prime Minister that this is one of the seven major commitments that the Liberal party set out during the campaign.
Yesterday, not in this House but after the debate in this House, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said that it was not the government's intention to establish the agency before the price rises which are going to be coming in June or July. Second, he said, and I quote: "The new energy watchdog will not even be asked for advice in this period, and in the period after July." Can I ask the Prime Minister which one of the seven commitments will be the next to go?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PETROLEUM PRICING AND AUDITING AGENCY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this commitment still stands. We want to set up that petroleum price auditing agency. We will do so, and it will be very important in the government's pursuit of its energy policy.

subsubtopic: MR. TAYLOR-ALLEGED CHANGE OF STATUTE BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to raise a question of privilege on the answer given by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) today. Just to recap the matter, my question was: Since when and under what authority can the cabinet change a statute by order in council? The answer given by the hon. minister was that the cabinet cannot change a statute by order in council.
Now I should like to look at the facts. First I should like to outline three very important axioms which are very relevant to this particular question. One is that the cabinet has no power except that given to it by the House of Commons. The second one is that the regulations must be based on laws passed by Parliament; they may be extensions but they may not change the law. The third one is that the House of Commons holds the ultimate power.
1 want to review the circumstances. After an agreement reached by the Government of Canada with the provinces, a bill was presented to the House of Commons which was passed. I should like to refer to chapter 37 of the Revised Statutes of Canada 1970. Section 3.(2) reads as follows:
The amount that may be paid to a province under subsection (1) in respect of a taxation year of a designated corporation is 95 per cent of that part of the income tax paid under part 1 of the Income Tax Act by the corporation for the year that is attributable to its gross revenue for the year-
There is a continuation but it does not change that particular point. So the statute definitely points out that 95 per cent of those moneys collected from the generation and sale in a province for distribution to the public of electrical energy or steam must be repaid to the province. That has been going on since the statute was passed right up until the order in council in question here.
I might say that in the 1978 budget of the hon. member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien) it was suggested that this would be changed. At that time I believe a bill received first reading. It was not proceeded with, so the law was not changed. But on March 27, 1980, the present cabinet passed the following order in council known as SOR/80-214 under the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act. It reads in part as follows:
May 9, 1980

His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue, pursuant to section 5 of the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act, is pleased hereby to amend the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Regulations, CRC, c. 1361, in accordance with the schedule hereto.
It continues:
Paragraph 3(2)(b) of the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Regulations is revoked and the following substituted therefor:
"(b) cause the product obtained by multiplying the estimated amount by the
fraction 50/95 to be paid to the province out of the Consolidated Revenue
Fund."
This is not an extension of the present act; this is a change of the amount entirely. This regulation was based on the act. The new regulation is not based on the act. I submit that one cannot change a regulation. As it is predicated upon the act- and the act indicates 95 per cent- the order in council certainly cannot change it, yet that is exactly what the order in council did.
As further reference that this is what the order in council did, the minister introduced a bill which received first reading on May 2. I should like to refer to clause 3 of that bill. The other clauses are not relevant to this particular point. Clause 3 reads as follows:
All that portion of subsection 3(2) of the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act-
Those are the ones I read to the House. It continues:
-preceding paragraph (a) thereof is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
So we are taking out of the act the section that the former regulation was based upon. It continues:
"(2) The amount that may be paid to a province under subsection (I) in respect of the 1966 to 1978 taxation years of a designated corporation is 95 per cent, and in respect of the 1979 and each subsequent taxation year of a designated corporation is 50 per cent, of that part of the income tax paid under part I of the Income Tax Act-
This will definitely change the legislation. It has not yet been changed, but it has received first reading in this House. 1 should like to point out that if the cabinet can change a law in this way, members of the House of Commons might just as well go home. To approve of changes in the law before the changes are made means that the House of Commons is being treated as a rubber stamp. We are violating one of the primary principles of representative government. The cabinet cannot spend money or use taxation without the consent of the House of Commons, yet that is exactly what has been done.
The bill goes a little further. Actually it places emphasis upon public ownership. It is a back door way of forcing the provinces into public ownership rather than private ownership. If that is the ultimate objective, the House will have to consider it. The law has not yet been changed, but the 95 per cent approved by the previous Liberal government, passed and approved by the House of Commons, has been violated by the present government. The minister said that we do not have the authority. In effect he has said, "Amen", that this is a question of privilege.
I want to suggest since this is a question of privilege that Madam Speaker approve it as such. I emphasize again that the
Privilege-Mr. Taylor
order in council changed the regulations based on the law which was in effect. It had no authority to change that amount. The House of Commons said 95 per cent; at that time the regulations indicated that it could be 95 per cent, but the minister in his order in council said, "No, we will change that basis and make it 50 per cent", which is completely different from the original act.
If the hon. Speaker finds this a valid question of privilege- and I think the minister has agreed already that it is-then I suggest that this question should be sent to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections to consider this whole matter, including the payment to the provinces of the moneys withheld under the authority of this order in council. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko):
That the matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections to consider this whole matter, including the payment to the provinces of the moneys withheld under the authority of that order in council.

Madam Speaker, I would like to deal briefly with this point which has been described as a question of privilege. It is obviously not a question of privilege. Whatever it is, it is not a question of privilege. It may be a matter of debate that can be dealt with when the bill is called for second reading.
The fact of the matter is that the bill-and of course, nobody questions that the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act provides that payments will be made at the 95 per cent level; there is no dispute about that-provides the minister with the power under the act to make payments at such time or times as he may determine, and the timing of the payments is provided for under regulations of the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act.
The regulations provide that payments can be made once each fiscal year in March. Each payment is composed of a
final adjustment in respect of a prior taxation year and an interim payment pending Revenue Canada's assessment of the tax return in respect of the current year. For example, the payment made in the 1979-80 fiscal year was made in March, 1980, and comprised a final adjustment in respect of the 1977 taxation year and an interim payment in respect of 1979.
Parliament was notified some time ago by the present Minister of Justice and (Mr. Chretien) that the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act would be amended and the decision was taken in the context of a $2.5 billion expenditure restraint program undertaken in the summer and fall of 1978. It was felt that in the light of this substantial expenditure restraint program, payments to the provinces, which constituted 20 per cent of total outlays, should bear part of the burden, and for that reason it was decided in fact to abolish the 95 per cent rebate by legislation and to make changes in the equalization program.
In fact, those two changes constitute, over the next two fiscal years, an expenditure amount of $1.5 billion. In other words, if this bill affecting the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act and equalization were not proceeded with the treasury would be attacked to the amount of $ 1.5 billion.
We are talking about the regularity of this procedure. These particular savings have been worked into the estimates that were prepared by the former government, and the former minister of finance has behaved in precisely the same way on the basis of the power that was given to him under the act; otherwise he would not be able to work these savings into his expenditure program.
The order in council was passed or the regulations were made under the authority and power given to Parliament, and by Parliament to the Minister of Finance, to make payments at such time or times as he may determine. I have stated that it is the practice each March to make a payment with respect to a past taxation year and an interim payment with respect to the current taxation year. We made an interim payment with respect to 1979, and that interim payment was 50 per cent.
If this bill is not passed when it comes to making the final payment for 1979-and the final payment is not due until 1982 under the practice-then, of course, it would have to be made at the 95 per cent level. The Minister of Finance is empowered to establish the timing, and the practice has been to make an interim payment. We are making an interim payment of 50 per cent for 1979. When the final payment comes due in 1982, under the practice which has been followed up to the present time, and if this bill is not passed, then of course the will of Parliament will be observed by the government in office and the full payment of 95 per cent will be made.
So the hon. member may raise a question of privilege in 1982 if the bill is not passed and if the government fails to make the payment in the amount of 95 per cent. I suggest that we defer the question of privilege until March, 1982, and it may be relevant at that time.

The House resumed, from Monday, April 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lapointe (Charlevoix) that Bill C-17, to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act, be read a second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity today to speak briefly on Bill C-17, a bill which gives some urgently needed recognition to one of our most vital sectors of our economy, that of small business.
There are over one million small businesses in Canada. Most of them have annual sales of less than $2 million and yet these small businesses were responsible last year for almost one-third of our GNP. Small business is highly labour intensive, employing 2.5 million or about 42 per cent of all business employment in Canada.
Small business means big business for Canada's banks. At the moment there are 430,000 loans made to small business enterprises which total $9 billion or 25 per cent of the total lending by banks. So to say that small business is an important part of the Canadian institution is simply an understatement. It is the backbone and financial base of every community, large or small, in this country, and it forms a very important segment of our national economy.
Yet, for some reason, in many political circles business is the least understood and the most maligned segment of our society. Some would have us believe that it is the businessman who is reaping rewards at the expense of the ordinary man who is struggling to make ends meet. The truth of the matter is that the goals and the aspirations of millions of Canadians in our work force depend on the success and the initiative of those engaged in small business.
In these difficult economic times, it is the small businessman who stands to lose everything that he has worked for. That is one of the reasons I and many of my colleagues entered politics. We saw those who had the most initiative, who took the most risks and who certainly worked the longest hours being pushed to the wall.
Our Liberal colleagues over the years have, because of increased spending on both domestic and foreign aid programs, loaded heavy taxes and endless regulations on to business, small and large. During the election campaign I spoke to many small businessmen in my community and we discussed their situation-the cost of filling in and filing forms, collecting and remitting taxes, applying for and paying licence fees, dealing with inspectors of all kinds, defending actions, and so on. It has been estimated that the cost of the "paperburden", as the present government so aptly termed it several years ago, comes to something like an average of $5,000 per year.
In addition, this past year business has had to cope with high interest rates, rates designed to fight inflation and uphold the value of the dollar but which add enormously to the cost of running a business.
Those with a cash flow problem-and let us be realistic, this includes practically every business-are caught. They must still stock their shelves or keep production going or they risk losing everything they have worked for. They cannot just go into hibernation while interest rates and costs are high and come out again when the situation brightens. Bills must still be
May 9, 1980

settled, payrolls must be met and taxes must be paid. And they usually are paid; the community benefits and people benefit and governments and banks benefit. Meanwhile, however, the debts of the small businessman are increasing as he strives to survive another month.
Small business is facing today a genuine economic crunch and we believe that the government has a special obligation to deregulate, unburden and generally help the small business community. Unlike large business, the small businessman does not always have the time to do the fancy, analytical work so necessary today, to examine economic trends, file briefs, make submissions to government to keep abreast with tax laws, exemptions and new regulations that continually come forth. A small firm can lose track of its real costs quickly in the maze of inflation and fast changing interest rates.
The individualistic small businessman, who has traditionally been the last to depend on others, is now looking to government to help solve a problem which is beyond his control and is not of his making. And why not? The government caused much of the problem by overspending, by artificially stimulating the economy, by buying and paying more than our markets could justify, and by borrowing so much in money markets to pay its debts that it crowded out legitimate business needs and enterprises.
I might also mention that, in addition, governments have failed to exercise control where control might well have been exercised. After all, if government is going to control and regulate business inside and out, it should at least be consistent and apply controls on the elements of cost created by itself, as well as costs relating to productivity. Fair wages, yes, but for fair production as well. We have a long way to go in this country in improving our labour cost versus productivity output. We have a long way to go towards balancing our position with other industrialized nations such as Japan and West Germany, which have nothing to compare with Canada's potential in national resources.
Our failure to date can hardly be laid at the door of the small businessman who is struggling against high wage costs, high taxes, and the high cost of operation, mostly brought about by government intrusion. Is it any wonder that almost 6,000 businesses went bankrupt in 1979, and that Ontario bankruptcies in the first two months of this year went up 25 per cent over the same period of last year?
Instead of making life difficult for small business, government should be injecting policies into the system to restore the basic incentive aspects to the business world. It is the responsibility of this House to enact legislation which will aid small business and we are supporting this bill because we believe it will help. We are glad the individual loan ceiling has been raised but we would have been happier with measures which would have lowered the interest rates on that increased loan amount.
The government has an obligation to fight, on behalf of the small businessman, the high interest rate problem, as the previous Conservative government did when it proposed the introduction of the small business debenture. This would have
Small Businesses Loans Act
allowed the small businessman to borrow up to half a million dollars at half the nominal rate of interest. This measure would have effectively lowered the after tax interest rate on such debts by about three percentage points, and this would have allowed many small and medium-sized companies to at least consider expansion programs which could result in further employment.
It was a great disappointment to me, when speaking to small business owners during the election campaign, to discover that they did not know about this excellent cost reduction measure which would have greatly aided their profit picture. Not only would it have made their businesses more profitable but it would have given small business an 8 per cent or 9 per cent competitive advantage over big business.
Hardly anyone was aware of this important measure, designed to keep small businesses healthy and vital and to maintain local employment in areas not protected by collective bargaining procedures. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I feel that in offering assistance to small business, the government must not only uncomplicate the procedures but must also improve the method of disseminating information all across this country so that business people are aware of the funds, loans, assistance programs and tax measures available to them.
I would like to stress the need for the speedy passage of Bill C-17. The Conservative party recognized the importance of small business in our economic community in its defeated budget of last December and was delighted to see so many of the measures proposed crop up again in the mini budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). It was our government which underlined the urgent need to alleviate the cash flow problems of the small business sector resulting from abnormally high interest rates, and we would certainly do nothing at this point to impede the passage of a bill which offers some relief to this country's small business people.
We strongly back the measures included in Bill C-17 but we must underline the need for the continuing support of this vital, mostly Canadian-owned segment of our economy. Bill C-17 is a start but the government must not stop here.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to address myself to this bill and to the House for the first time in the Thirty-second Parliament. I am also pleased to see that the new government is again implementing initiatives first voiced by the last government. I, of course, refer to our stated intention of aiding small business, by recognizing the importance of small business to the national economy.
For the benefit of those who are unaware of some of the facts concerning small business in Canada, I should like to point out that there are approximately 600,000 small firms in business in Canada. In combination with other small entrepreneurs such as professionals and commissioned sales personnel, there are a total of over 800,000 enterprises which could be described as comprising the small business community in our great country of Canada.
In terms of total national employment and production, the small business community plays a substantial role in the

May 9, 1980
Small Businesses Loans Act
working of the economy. The production of goods and services by small business enterprises accounts for 20 per cent of the value of all goods and services produced in Canada.
Clearly, a sector of the economy which produces such a substantial component of the gross national product must be counted as a vital component of the total commercial and industrial mosaic in Canada. In terms of achieving national goals such as increased employment, increased real earnings and dimished regional disparities, the potential contribution from small enterprise is indeed immense. It is difficult, in fact, to see how such goals could be achieved without enhanced small business participation.
A major interest of mine, in contemplating the benefits of small business to our economy and national life, is the contribution made by the tourist industry. This industry leads to an increased understanding and awareness of each other's unique contribution to Canada, and, as such, is a strong bond in our confederation. Moreover, of the 800,000 small businesses in Canada, fully 80,000 or 10 per cent are involved in some way in the tourist trade.
In 1978, the Canadian tourism industry was worth $11 billion to Canada, or about 5 per cent of our gross national product. Of this amount, nearly $9 billion came from the spending of Canadians travelling right here in Canada, while more than $2 billion came from the spending of visitors to Canada from foreign countries.
This industry accounts for over one million jobs in Canada, or one in every 11 working Canadians. The majority of foreign visitors come from the United States, our great neighbour to the south. Two-thirds of our international travel revenue comes from this source, while overseas visitors account for roughly one-third of our foreign exchange revenue from travel. Tourism is Canada's sixth largest earner of foreign exchange, and it is the world's fastest growing industry.
As I mentioned. Mr. Speaker, the Canadian tourism industry involves seme 80,000 businesses which are widely dispersed across our nation. There are about 20,000 hotels, lodges, cabins, motels and campgrounds, an estimated 43,000 restaurants, a myriad of events and attractions, as well as facilities such as parks, historic sites and marinas.
Furthermore, it has been forecast that tourism will be one of the world's largest industries, if not the largest, by the year 2000. If current growth rates of approximately 10 per cent per annum continue, very nearly two billion people will be travelling by the year 2000. That means for every two people travelling today, there will be three in the year 2000. Total worldwide tourist revenues will rise to nearly $2,000 billion by the year 2000.
In terms of the total numbers of travellers, the future looks like a marketer's paradise. Canada will undoubtedly share in the growth of worldwide tourism, and it is well placed to benefit from these faster growth rates.
However, in order for the tourist industry in Canada to benefit fully from this expected increase in travel, certain programs and opportunities must be in place to support and promote the travel industry in Canada. That is why, with certain reservations, I am happy that this bill has been introduced and that it will make financing of loans of up to $100,000 available. For in order to exploit the growth in tourism, Canadian facilities must grow and improve, and as we know that will require money.
If I may, I would like to refer to a report of the Tourism Sector Consultative Task Force on the Canadian tourism industry. The publication is dated July 12, 1978. At page 33 under the title of C-9 in connection with the Small Businesses Loans Act, it says:
-in connection with the Small Businesses Loans Act, the limits should be raised to $250,000 (amount of loans outstanding) and $2,000,000.00 (gross revenue). There may be a problem of chartered banks requiring mortgages for a small business loan. They should accept a second mortgage as the loan is government guaranteed.
So we see that $100,000 is not too much money, and it is probably insufficient for many businesses to carry on.
However, I do have some misgivings about the Small Businesses Loans Act. The fact is that this program has not been fully promoted and advertised. The majority of small business persons are unaware of the Small Businesses Loans Act and, indeed, are confused by the multitude of programs available, either provincially or federally.
These programs, I am sure you will agree, Mr. Speaker, offer many financial alternatives to small businesses. In point of fact, however, without adequate dissemination of information on particular programs, such as the Small Businesses Loans Act, the small business person is confused and perplexed in an already complex financial marketplace.
Therefore, my recommendation would be to make the small business person more aware of the programs available by advertising in trade magazines or by information supplied to the accounting profession, who are often the first turned to when a question of financing is raised.
The purpose of this proposed advertising would be two-fold. Not only would the business person be apprised of the funding available, but this knowledge would arm him in his dealings with the banks and other lending institutions. For it is well known in the business community that the banks are reluctant to inform loan applicants of this funding option.
This is not because of any inherent risk in lending funds with the federal government acting as guarantor although, if the federal deficit continues to increase as forecast by the infamous mini-budget, that could become a real consideration. It is because, as in so many other situations, businesses both large and small do not have the time, and many times do not have the patience or the resources, to indulge in the vast amount of paperwork which dealing with the government entails.
I have had constituents who have told me that banks just cannot be bothered to go through all the nuisance of filling out forms with all the detail that government demands. I ask you,
May 9, 1980

Mr. Speaker, what is the use of having this program if the banks, who are to administer it, would rather not inform their clients of its availability because the benefit to the bank is outweighed by the cost, in terms of time needed to comply with the government demand for information? If the bank is willing to lend the money, using the criteria that prudent lending practices dictate, why is it necessary that this government form be so complex and so demanding?
This is a problem that is not restricted to those who live in my riding of Erie. It is a problem that is seen across Canada and recognized as a hindrance to business by many, chief among them the Canadian Federation of Independent Business which has made strong representations in the past to the federal government on this problem.
The situation is so bad that the professional trade magazine for accountants counsels its members to do an end run around the banks and other lending institutions by applying for a loan, having it approved, and then requesting that the loan be considered under the Small Businesses Loans Act.
This government, who in the past started the "office of paperburden", should be aware of the difficulties encountered by small business in availing themselves of funding, strictly because of the complexity of the application for that funding. If this government indeed means what it says about helping small business, this is an obvious first step to take. Eliminate the paper burden, advertise the Small Businesses Loans Act extensively, and this recommended legislation will be a good start to encouraging and promoting the cause of small business in Canada.

the general context of the review we are now doing of the funding problems of small business.

Others of my colleagues opposite used this debate on Bill C-17 to deal more generally with the interest rate problems and all the difficulties facing small businesses. I noticed more particularly, Mr. Speaker, the very lively and convincing speech by our colleague from Burlington (Mr. Kempling) who referred to the difficulties and annoyances small businessmen can face in Canada when they decide to apply for those programs established by any level of government. I can assure my colleague from Burlington that we will not limit our efforts to reducing administrative formalities and problems caused to Canadian businessmen by red tape. Indeed, as he requested in his speech, we have explained the Small Businesses Loans Act in a booklet and 300,000 copies have been distributed in 1979; furthermore, the banks are trying to improve and develop their information system so that businessmen can be made aware of that very useful and very important program as a development tool for small businesses.

However, I do not think that Bill C-17 is the proper channel through which to tackle the high interest rates which Canadian businessmen have to pay. As all hon. members know as well as I do, Mr. Speaker, as late as yesterday we saw that for four weeks now the interest rate has maintained a downward trend and I hope that will help Canadian businessmen.
As mentioned by the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid) earlier this morning, 1 think the proposal made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in his economic statement a few weeks ago, that is the business development bond, will allow them in the short run to face the high interest rates which have been especially hard on small business.

1 would like to come back more precisely to one remark made by our colleague, the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson). In his remarks he said that clause 4 of the SBLA bill would allow the maximum aggregate number of guarantees to increase from $600 million to $675 million up to

There is no way an additional $75 million is going to be guaranteed within the next 30 days or so, and therefore I strongly suspect that this is a cover-up and that loans have already been guaranteed in excess of the $600 million allowed by the law.

AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD The House resumed from Wednesday, April 30, consideration of the motion of Mr. Axworthy that Bill C-19, to amend
May 9, 1980
the Employment Tax Credit Act, be read the second time and referred to Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Speaker,
I am pleased to be able to resume debate on Bill C-19 after an adjournment of several days. I should like to take the opportunity in the course of my intervention to expand upon some of the concerns I have as a Canadian about the larger questions of the current state of our economy, and what 1 see as a lack of action on behalf of the government and of the minister who introduced this bill in coming to grips with the much needed solutions to these problems.
The bill before us, entitled "an act to amend the Employment Tax Credit Act", is merely an extension of an existing program which was introduced as a temporary program, and for that reason we will extend it for one more year. Government members opposite have made a great deal in recent months of the number of jobs that have been created through programs of employment tax credit and the like.
I think that Canadians would like to know what follow-up statistics show as to whether jobs created by this type of a temporary initiative are permanent or whether those jobs self-destruct shortly after the benefits terminate. We understand that the extension for another year will allow another 50,000 new jobs to be created, but we have to look to the next year with a great degree of discomfort in recognizing that, by the end of 1980, we may again have more than 1.2 million people unemployed in this country. I think we should really be asking the minister-and I hope we will ask him-in committee and on future occasions, what other initiatives he has been able to impose upon his cabinet colleagues to convince the government to deal with the growing and horrendous problem of unemployment which is likely to occur in this country, if the economy goes in the direction that many prognosticators predict it will.
So the first question I ask is: Will these be temporary or permanent jobs? Second, will the conditions of eligibility- that is, that the employer has to state that these positions will be surplus to the normal requirement-and the atmosphere which is likely to prevail in such circumstances, reduce inefficiency and initiative on the part of the employer and the workers, in the sense that it means essentially that we will get more bodies to do the same job?
If the government is going to give employers back some of their tax money or allow them to keep it to hire people to do tasks surplus to the normal requirement, perhaps that might be regarded as having a demoralizing effect on fellow employees and on the attitude of the company in pursuing competitive instincts. Of course, we want to know whether, and how, abuses are prevented in which the employer signs a declaration leaving the impression he is embarking on a new initiative when, in effect, he may just be filling a position which he would otherwise have had to meet from his existing cash flow. So there are a number of questions that might be asked of the minister and I trust we will have a chance to pursue these questions in committee.
Employment Tax Credit Act
However, I should like to get off that point and on to the main thrust of my intervention to indicate that this is indeed a short-term initiative. It is as if the minister were pretending he was feeding peanuts to a friendly elephant in a situation where that elephant is no longer an elephant but has become a hungry lion. If the minister is not too careful, he may lose more than his arm.
The scenario facing this country in the next few months, I think, results from an attitude on the part of the government- not only the politicians but the bureaucrats who design systems-that we can cater to every human need by throwing more money at it or by designing a new government program, establishing a new government department, and proliferating the notion that the government can take over whenever the private sector fails. It is true that we need more in the way of tax measures and less in the way of government make-work programs. As this is a tax measure I applaud it, albeit as only a temporary initiative.
I believe that the country is in a state of crisis largely because the private sector in this country has become seriously demoralized. What do we need to do to re-establish a buoyant and productive economy in Canada? I believe that the past decade of Liberal rule has broken the spirit of the private sector economy, especially the small business sector, such as manufacturing, merchandising, construction, farming, fishing and the like. A government which takes with one hand and hands back to someone else with the other sooner or later demoralizes the producers in society. Indeed, we will have a degree of equality where we may all enjoy the same comforts of life, but those comforts, in the final analysis, will be less in total than if we continued to encourage individual initiative and the instinct to rise to the height of challenge, to be entrepreneurial and to create an expanding economy.
Therefore, I really believe there are two key facets to the problem of unemployment in Canada today. First, we have the facet that has been created by more than a decade of government which pursues a Liberal socialist philosophy and which is destroying the private sector instinct to build our country.
Second, we have a government which has set a bad standard for the private sector to emulate in terms of the manner in which they have managed the economy. I would go so far as to suggest that the monetary socialist approach that has been taken to the conduct of our economic affairs in this country reflects a degree of incompetence and a lack of common sense. There is little comprehension of the tools required to encourage the growth, development and entrepreneurial instincts of those who would build their future, without having to be subject to the heavy hand of government.
I want to give a few examples to illustrate that thesis, but first I should like to return to my first point. I think there is a philosophy afoot in this country. I do not have to think that; it is obvious. It is manifest in the attitude that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) has taken toward the resource-owning provinces. It is an attitude which is based on the so-called concept of sharing.
902

May 9, 1980
Employment Tax Credit Act
I put a lot of stock in the Judeo-Christian values which suggest that we should be our brother's keeper. I think most members in the House do so too. There is genuine hardship and genuine need in society and we all do have a collective responsibility to respond. But the concept of sharing as revealed by government members opposite and by my friends to the left has become a dogma. I would go so far as to say it could be called the Robin Hood concept of sharing. In fact, the dictionary will confirm that "sharing" means the "giving and receiving of wealth or goods for the common good, in a framework of generosity".
I believe that it takes an atmosphere of generosity and good will if this notion of sharing is to work, the notion which was so fully reflected in the throne speech and which stated that we must have justice for all. I suggest that in our quest for justice and equality we can go too far; we can go so far as to destroy the spirit of individuals and of regions to build and progress on their own account.
1 believe it is true that the resources of individual regions are given to them as the basis for building their local economies. That title to resource ownership has been granted since the time of confederation. Indeed, there was some dispute in the House earlier today about the means by which the government opposite is intervening and abrogating that right which the provinces have enjoyed for more than a century. The notion that resources can be confiscated from one sector of society or from one individual in society and assigned to another can be carried too far. As a consequence, I believe the private sector, the business sector and particularly the small business sector in this country are terribly demoralized. We will not eliminate that problem by increasing taxes, by imposing upon them more bureaucracy, more red tape and form filling, but indeed by doing the exact opposite; that is, by getting off their backs and giving them an opportunity to grow and prosper in this country.
I should like to come to the second point of my thesis. Aside from being over-zealous in the pursuit of this notion of sharing, the government, the monetary socialists, have really mishandled the economic affairs of this country. There is a lack of common sense in the manner by which they have husbanded the taxpayers' hard-earned resources. We read a lot these days about something called the Laffer curve.
I do not want to bore the House with technical descriptions, except to indicate that there is one theory in society which indicates that the higher the tax level is raised, the more revenue the government gets for the purpose of delivering the programs it would like to deliver. That is, the greater the taxation becomes as a percentage of take-home income or the gross national product of the country, the more revenue will flow to government and the more opportunity the government will have to do things; to reinvest that revenue to provide some form of incentive or initiative in some other sector of the economy. Increasingly it is becoming evident that that type of a straight line relationship just does not follow common sense,
nor does it conform with thousands of years of experience. In fact, if the percentage of the wealth of the economy or of the average take-home pay of individuals that the government takes in the form of taxation is increased without limit, there is a level of taxation where we begin to destroy the incentive for individuals who want to build collectively for the common good of society. If one continues to increase taxes above that level, the revenue flowing to government, and indeed the gross national product of a country, will begin to subside and fall very quickly to a very low value. This is the principle behind the so-called Laffer curve.
When one is beyond that point at which the level of taxation has exceeded the optimum one for producing the best delivery of services and the healthiest economy, or when people are being surtaxed to too great an extent, one will find that further increases in taxes do nothing more than further demoralize the economy. In fact, in this situation tax reductions are the only way to stimulate the economy and to put us back on an even keel. If we look at the evidence, it is clear that the percentage of taxation as a fraction of the gross national product in this country has doubled since 1970. I believe, that we have gone beyond the point where further increases in taxes can be regarded as a benefit to the economy and to the initiatives the government might take. In fact, the present tax levels are probably destructive to the economic progress of our country.
This little discourse on the mechanism of the Laffer curve tells us, I believe, that we are heading into difficult economic times and ever-increasing unemployment, simply because we do not understand the basic, common sense rules of economics.
I should like to point now to some information which came to my attention recently. This information is not widely known. It has to do with the magnitude of Canada's borrowing. We have heard a lot of debate in recent weeks about the additional deficit which will result because the Liberals opposite are reluctant to face up to the fact that we must pay for what we consume or else our children will pay it for it in the future. So they do not mind holding down oil prices artificially and accumulating an additional $2 billion of federal deficit for 1980. They feel that it is all right that our children pay for that some time further down the road.
Of course, that is just one example of the way in which this government continues to enlarge the federal deficit to the point where in 1979-80 the former Liberal government projected to spend 20 per cent more than they would receive in revenue. But when the Progressive Conservative government took office and presented its budget, we had reduced that government deficit to less than 14 per cent of government spending. Now, as a consequence of the mini non-budget presented recently in this House, we are back to a situation where the government will again incur 20 per cent more in terms of spending than it will receive by way of income during the present fiscal year.
The budget of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) indicated that within five years a conservative government would reduce our deficit to less than 6 per cent of programmed expenditure. It is a travesty, a condemnation of the government opposite, that they will not present five-year
May 9, 1980

projections as to where this country is going. They are reluctant, they are hesitant. They know where they are leading us but they are afraid to admit to the public at large that they are bankrupting this country.
I think it is important that we plan ahead, that we respect the resources of the people who foot the bill and display some consideration for the consequences which massive deficit financing will have on the economic strength of Canada. To highlight that point I want to refer to data taken from the annual reports of the World Bank which showed something rather alarming. These reports indicate that in the years from 1974 to 1979 Canada has borrowed more money in the form of foreign loans and international bond issues than any other country in the world. 1 do not mean on a per capita basis; 1 mean that Canada is borrowing more money than any other nation in the world. Sure, it is great to live in Canada, but how is it that we can be so foolish as to borrow at such a rate that in 1976 we borrowed 26 per cent of all the moneys borrowed by all the countries of the world? The average between 1974 and 1979, as reported in the annual reports of the World Bank, is 18 per cent of all the world's borrowing, incurred in the name of Her Majesty the Queen on behalf of those of us here, our families and our children. Since 1974 Canada has been the world leader in total borrowings.
When we listen to the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) coming into the House and telling us that because of high interest rates Canada will now incur at least $500 million more in deficits as a result of the carrying charges on that borrowing which was not anticipated two or three months ago, it shows how vulnerable this country has become to international forces and how dependent we are on the wiles and economic circumstances of countries and situations beyond our control.
It might interest members to know that in fact Canada's borrowing is larger than that of France or Japan by a considerable degree. In 1976 Canada borrowed $9.5 billion on international markets, while the next highest borrower, France, borrowed only $2.8 billion. We borrowed $9.5 billion out of a total of $34 billion borrowed by all the countries of the world. Indeed, we are borrowing almost a quarter of the world deficit!
Is it not time to take this matter under consideration and change the course of this country? On a per capita basis Canada borrowed almost 25 times as much as Japan, and in 1976 Japan was the world's third highest borrower. In 1978 Canada borrowed $4.85 billion out of a world total of $36 billion. Japan borrowed only $2.8 billion with a population five times larger.
I see that you are shedding a tear or two, Mr. Speaker, and I think we all should. I am citing this evidence to show that government members opposite have no common sense when it comes to the question of managing the wealth of this country and its tremendous potential. Here we are going off to Mexico signing contracts for oil, we go off to Saudi Arabia and elsewhere to assure sources of supply, when we have the supply
Employment Tax Credit Act
right within our own country. The present government is, indeed, assuring non-security of supply by its very actions.
We also have this question of high interest rates, and I have to reflect on a personal perspective which has probably been mirrored by what has happened in the last couple of weeks with the collapse of the interest rate levels. When Mr. Bouey, the governor of the Bank of Canada, came before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs last fall, he told us that we had to maintain high interest rates in order to keep inflation under control, and the reason for that was that we depend so much for the commodities we consume and use in our homes on "imported products".
Secondly, governor Bouey said that our Canadian plant capacity was saturated. Therefore, if we did not keep interest rates high the Canadian dollar would fall, thus encouraging more inflation because of the higher costs of imported goods which we rely upon. He said we had to discourage that and keep inflation under control.
Some very prominent people in this country associated with the Canadian Institute for Economic Policy-and all members of Parliament received this report released on April 22, 1980- recently took the following position, and let me quote:
The Bank of Canada's policy for reducing inflation- tight money and high interest rates-might have had some justification if the inflation had been caused by an overly expanded economy. But the Canadian economy has not been overheated. Therefore, the Bank's policy has been ill-advised. It has not been successful, and, if persisted in, will be no more successful in the future.
I am pleased to see, therefore, that there has been some change of heart on behalf of the governor of the Bank of Canada. I do not think that the current trend is entirely consequential upon the tumbling interest rates in the United States. I hope we are soon going to wake up to the realization that we do have the opportunity to control our own economy. It is shortsighted to say we cannot increase our own plant capacity. It is shortsighted to say we should continue to enjoy all of the comforts of these things we like to buy from offshore and to travel extensively outside the country when, indeed, a lower dollar, if that had to be the consequence of lower interest rates, would offer a tremendously healthy advantage for our economy. That point also is clearly stated in the report which I have cited.
Who wrote it?

If hon. members opposite wish me to indicate the author, as they have requested, let me say that the author of this report was a former Liberal finance minister who says the Bank of Canada is wrong, that the Liberal government is wrong and has been wrong for many years, and that it is time we realized that the only way to an independent and healthy economy is to recognize that high interest rates in fact increase inflation, increase bankruptcies and impose a hardship on individual businesses that operate within our country.
Now, if you look at the budget brought down by the former minister of finance on December 11, Mr. Speaker, you will note that the mortgage tax credit program would, indeed, have represented a subsidy on interest rates to the tune of 25 per

May 9, 1980
Employment Tax Credit Act
cent. Members opposite do not want to admit that and neither do our NDP friends to our left, but a 25 per cent tax credit on mortgage payments is a 25 per cent subsidy on mortgage interest rates. That would have ensured that the forest industry would not be collapsing in western Canada and in other parts of the country. It would have assured the construction industry, the real estate industry and the home furnishing industry a much healthier position in Canada today. This would have reduced the cost of a 15 per cent mortgage on renewal to something less than 12 per cent. It is utterly irresponsible for members opposite to have taken the approach they did in condemning that initiative.
On the other side of the question, they like to make a great point of the fact that the mortgage tax credit was going to cost the government something. Actually it was a matter of leaving revenue in the pockets of the people who earned it and were entitled to it. It is the opposite of the Robin Hood philosophy.
On the other hand, the Liberals said that to pay for that cost we were going to increase the price of oil. We were in fact going to increase the price of oil-to a lesser degree than they will in fact have to increase it, inevitably-in order to encourage conservation, and also in order to encourage employment in this country in the private sector of the petroleum industry, in exploration, in the steel fabricating and steel rolling industries, and in terms of all of those supporting industries, including the shipbuilding industry, which would be part of our attempt to develop our own energy resources.
What I am saying is that higher oil prices and a mortgage tax credit program both would have created more jobs than we have in Canada today and would not have cost the Government of Canada one nickel. In fact, all of these additional jobs would have reduced the burden on the unemployment insurance fund and would have increased the flow of income tax revenue to the federal coffers. Without any net change in the existing revenue picture, the Government of Canada and the people of this country would be facing a much healthier economy as we move into the 1980s than we are as a consequence of the Liberal government's retrograde policies; its ill-conceived and nonsensical plans.
Let me deal now with some of the consequences of the government's incompetence in my own riding. I should like to cite a few circumstances that have arisen over the past two or three years. Let me read first from a letter dated April 27 1980, received from a constituent. Reading from its body, it states:
It is with regret that I have to inform you that Max Sibbeiee Aircraft Tires Ltd. is forced to close down its retreading plant as of May 1. 1980.
Due to rising costs, stiff competition from the United States companies and the complete lack of protection from the federal and provincial governments, another Canadian company has gone down.
I should like to tell hon. members a little of the history of this situation. Some three years ago the owner of this small business, the only western Canadian business engaged in the retreading of aircraft tires, was placed under some pressure from a California firm to stop retreading tires and to merely import and distribute their product. At the same time, the
Canadian federal government was financing the establishment in Ontario of a retreading plant in the name of that same California firm, and that government-supported retreading plant, of course, got all the Air Canada business. My constituent found that his area of the retreading market was reduced, but rather than accept the offer from the U.S. firm to become merely a warehouse for their tires, he came to the hon. government House leader in the other place, a well-known Liberal politician from western Canada, and asked if the Senator could help him obtain some tariff protection so that this company from California would not be able to compete unfavourably with him, allowing him to stay in the business of continuing to supply tires to the Department of National Defence, CP Air and other airlines operating in western Canada.
Unfortunately, my constituent had a very frustrating and unsatisfactory time with that particular member of the government. Subsequently he learned that if he was to stay in business he had to purchase a machine called a holographic tire testing machine, which he could buy only in the United States, in order to examine every retreaded tire he produced to ensure there were no imperfections or defects. One wonders why this new standard was suddenly imposed. Nonetheless, upon purchasing this equipment, which cost several hundred thousand dollars, he was immediately slapped with an import duty for bringing that piece of equipment in from the U.S., although it was not available in Canada.
He appealed successively to ministers of this government but received no satisfaction and no agreement to his request that the import duties assessed be refunded. So on the one hand he got no protection from imported products that competed with his product line and, on the other hand, when he was required to upgrade his own manufacturing capacity, he had to pay import duty on the equipment he had to purchase from the U.S. in order to stay in business.
As a consequence of the recent action of this government, in denying this man some rebate of the duty on this very sophisticated piece of equipment, his business has collapsed and 50 people are out of work. There is something wrong with the attitude of a government which does not pay attention to the importance of building enterprise in this country and to giving special consideration to small businesses and employers such as my constituent.
I would like now to cite another situation which has developed in my riding. It is with respect to the potato processing industry. Three years ago an entrepreneur in my riding had just put the finishing touches on an $8 million plant for processing french fried potatoes into packaged form for use in commercial and retail outlets. Around that time he discovered that the federal government had awarded a large DREE grant to a company in Manitoba to produce the same product.
I tried at that time to find out from the officials in DREE what market studies had been done to determine the impact of the competitive imbalance which would result, because of the
