They go on to list the economic benefits, but this is where we get great industrial benefits and meaningful job creation. This study also points out the following:
These programs would promote lively residential fringes and recreational areas circling the north and east parts of the downtown, and will promote the fullest range of urban activities that belong in the centre core. They would have no serious or harmful effects on the development of suburban areas, however, it will mean a lesser function for the suburban shopping centres.
So you can see how extensive this was.
If the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is not familiar with this study, he can check with the officials in his department because four were involved from the Department of Transport.
1 hope that this will clear up the need for more studies, and 1 hope we will not be reading more newspaper articles such as this. There is a headline in this article referring to the Minister of Employment and Immigration which reads, "Minister Raids Ottawa for Relocation Funding". This is where he has gone wrong.
As 1 pointed out earlier, this whole approach has been in reverse. Now that we have gone this far-we have discussed it-it is a serial in the daily newspapers, I hope that he will now take some time to meet with the President of the Treasury board and the Minister of Finance to work on obtaining the $80 million. This ridiculous proposal from the Minister of DREE (Mr. De Bane) for $5 million a year for five years is the most idiotic proposal I have heard in this whole series since it started about 15 months ago.
They lead with the hind end.

Yes, as the hon. member says, they lead with the hind end. So let us stop the nonsense. Let us not have any more press conferences and meetings until the minister can come to Winnipeg and say, "I have met with the Minister of Finance, I have met with the President of the Treasury board, and I have the support of the cabinet. They have finally agreed to supply us with $84 million because we will have a meaningful program which will create employment." If he does that, he will go down in history as a hero and he will
Employment Tax Credit Act
make up for the blundering through which he has led us in the last 15 months.
I hope the minister is listening with interest to what I have said this afternoon because we are behind him on this. We all want rail relocation and we do not want to be talking about this two years from now and to find out that the Arlington and Salter Street bridges are closed and the only route remaining is Main Street-he knows how narrow it is-and all we have is McPhillips Street at the other end. People in Manitoba will be after him wanting to tar and feather him if he does not take some decisive action in the next two weeks.
Mr. Speaker, I will address my remarks to you, sir. I hope you will remain in the chair.
He has just left.

I see that one of ours is in the chair for a change.
This legislation on the employment tax credit is, in my view, representative of Liberal programs over the last 12 years. It is another band-aid, another fix-up, a little piece here, another little piece there. Because of our defeat by members on the other side, we have not continued with construction. House construction has stopped. They would not have needed to worry about the tax credit if they had allowed construction to go on. We were thrown out for that.
The second thing the Liberals have done since they have been in power is in connection with the synthetic oil production which our government was going to act upon so as to make certain that this country became self-sufficient and so as to provide jobs, not only in Alberta but many more in Ontario and Quebec. Because of force majeure provisions that the government has put in, employment is down again in Ontario. This attitude amazes me, being from Ontario. They talk about money for Chrysler, money for Quebec for manufacturing vehicles, but they do not want any production in Alberta so as to make us oil self-sufficient and create labour in this country which is so desperately needed.
Disgusting.

Yes, it is disgusting, as an hon. member says. They boast about not re-introducing the 18-cent tax and killing the mortgage tax deductibility. The 18-cent tax would have allowed us to make this country not only oil self-sufficient but also manufacturing self-sufficient and create employment. We would not need these programs if we had a program that would overcome the unemployment problem before you start.
1 congratulate the minister on the employment tax credit program. It is part of the total program, but it is only a little piece-it does not solve the problem. It does not help those big companies to expand and enlarge in a realistic way. It is a band-aid, a patch work. I urge the minister to work with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) and the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Lapointe), and come up with a solution.

May 9, 1980
Employment Tax Credit Act
This is only part of the total economic package. Our government put together a total economic package which would have made this country solve the employment problems. Let the minister look at it, copy some more of it, or take the whole thing and do it properly. I wish he would admit that we had a good program. We had an economic program which they could go on with. They took part of it. Let them finish the job and steal the rest of it. Let them do it properly. We had a good program. Let them give some incentive to the private sector, let them not always create government work. This is not working. During the election one party came up with the slogan "Control government, not people". 1 maintain that that is what we must do. By continuing to put in these patchwork programs, we will not be solving our over-all problems.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) stated that there must be a gradual reduction of inflation and interest rates and that this is the only viable solution to this problem. Why does he not practise this at home in Ottawa instead of spending more of our money? Let the people spend it, let the individual, the private sector spend it, not the government. We are compounding our deficits; our children are going to suffer. The government is not supporting any proper program, it is only creating a patchwork of problems. How will it get the 50 per cent equity in our oil industry? There is only one way to do it and that is to nationalize it, which will again mean bigger government. It is the same as they did with PetroCan. They owe $2 billion now for PetroCan. They can go and borrow another $2 billion. Then we will not stand at an 18 per cent average of world borrowing; we will stand at 50 per cent of world borrowing.
What happened to all the tax breaks? When will they bring in some tax breaks for working Canadians? We have seen the working people worried about unemployment and their retirement. When will we care about working Canadians? They are the persons who are the guts of this country. We must pay attention to them. My party provided for working Canadians. We provided mortgage interest and property tax deductibility to give them a break against punitive tax costs.
I should like to refer to a document which contains just general things that could be done by this government. They should reduce the burden on the economy by reducing government. They should reduce the size of the public service. They should disseminate Crown corporations and Crown agencies. They should get some initiative back into the private sector to generate growth and jobs for Canadians. They should do it through the private sector, not through government subsidy. They should help Canadians to get a stake in this country, not only through their own homes but through ownership of stocks of Canadian corporations. I plead with the government to do something about getting the private initiative back into this country. This is part of a program from which I am reading. They should help the regions of this country. There are regions which need more support than other regions. They should look at it realistically. They should not just pick the little pieces
here and the little pieces there. It must be done on a total global basis.
It is pornographic.

It is not pornographic. That is what I would consider their program to be. I will not use the term, but they are that. They are doing nothing to solve the problems of the citizens and the entrepreneurs of this country.
What about oil self-sufficiency? I have heard the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) talk flim-flam, mish-mash or whatever it is about this subject. What will they do? If they direct their energy toward oil self-sufficiency and manufacturing self-sufficiency, they would not need employment tax credit programs. That would solve it.
The five points I mentioned happen to be statements from the Speech from the Throne of the Thirty-first Parliament. They should steal more of our ideas. They were good ideas. They were excellent ideas that were going to turn this country around. Dealing with the oil industry, every time a synthetic oil plant was built approximately $3 billion would remain in Ontario because of related services. I never worked out how much it would be in Quebec. Alberta does not have these services. The services flow back to the east, and it is the east that is so concerned. They should look at the total picture. They should not worry about who is getting what here and there.
An example is DREE programs. The money usually flows back to the industrial base of the country. We know that it does not all stay where the DREE grants are given. It flows back. I am just saying that they should look beyond what they have in their employment tax credit program. They should develop a total program. They should develop an over-all strategy, an employment strategy. They have the people who can do it. They have the ideas they can steal and they have a lot of ideas they can create themselves.
They sure know how to steal ideas.

Working Canadians-and I must say that we contributed toward this-have been left with two pleasures. I am talking about the unemployed man whom they are going to help to get back to work. They picked two things out of our budget, which I do not think was very good. The man has two pleasures left-one, his beer, and two, his cigarettes. Now they are trying to tax that away from him. At least we were including that as part of a total package. It was relative to the 5 per cent tax on corporations. It was relative to the mortgage interest and property tax deductibility which would have created jobs. It was relative to the realistic price of oil. If there was a realistic price of oil, they would not need employment tax credit. They would have this country running, operating and working, and they would be as proud to be a Canadian as 1 am. We could have been proud. We should get back on the track. Instead of bringing in partial legislation, they should bring in a total package.
May 9, 1980
You have to know where you are going to do that.

Where is the youth employment program? There is double the number of people in our youth corps, that is, under 25 years of age. There is double the number there. Where is the youth program? Where is an apprenticeship program? Last year in Oshawa they were crying for trained personnel. They had to go to Britain to bring these people in. There is a program to which the government should be able to address itself to get these young people working, involved and particularly to give them a skill. This cannot be done by $2.50 an hour for so many weeks, or whatever it is. I am talking about learning a trade that may take a year, two years or three years, but it must be done realistically. This is a major program which the minister could introduce. It could do great things to solve the unemployment levels of this country and to get the country working again.
The government seems to spend more time investigating successful Canadian corporations to see what it can get out of them. Ministers should be encouraging those companies to develop additional manufacturing facilities. Instead they put punitive taxes on them. They do not give Canadians the opportunity to invest in those companies. They do not give the employees of those companies an opportunity. 1 am saying that they should get on with it. They should give them a greater chance to get this country going and to get private initiative going. That is what is missing. That is where the employment problems will be solved. They would get the country working-oil would be produced and iron ingots would be converted to steel products. They would have the country moving. We are just hewers of wood and haulers of water. It is time to change that. That is where an employment program could be very worth while.
As I have mentioned before, I maintain that it must be part of a total economic package. The government working together with others could accomplish this, but I plead with them not to do patchwork solutions to major unemployment problems. They should do a total package or a total frame. They should do a whole program. They have the time. They have the experience. They have a lot of friends. They have a lot of friends in the public service who have many ideas. An example is right in the Department of Communications with which 1 was fortunate enough to be connected. They are not addressing the problems there. There is employment there, but there are employment problems there too. I acknowledge that we should be addressing those.
As we are moving into the electronic age very quickly, they must realize that there will be a change in the labour force. There will be a reduction of people in the service industry. They will be investing an amount similar to the $50,000 per working person that is being spent in the manufacturing sector, or even the $70,000 per working person in the farming sector, instead of the $3,000 per working person which they are spending in the service industry at the present time. If we do not move on that now, we will be dependent upon Japanese and United States products. We have high technology.
Business of the House
The public service with which they are now working has some very fine people who have developed high technology. They should find out about Telidon. Find out about Annex C, D and E. Those are job-creating works. Get the money put in there and become numero uno in this country with high technology; we have it, we are not using it and we are not investing it. This is one of the greatest areas that can be developed in this country, and it is probably one of the most important places in this century.
Four o'clock.
Thank you, Mr. Minister. May I call it four o'clock?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED STEP TO PROVIDE FOR AMENDMENT IN CANADA
speechtext:
That an humble address be presented to Her Majesty the Queen in the following words:
To the Queen's Most Excellent Majesty:
Most Gracious Sovereign:
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the Commons of Canada in Parliament assembled, humbly approach Your Majesty, praying that you may graciously be pleased to cause a measure to be laid before the Parliament of the United Kingdom to be expressed as follows:

maintopic: AN ACT TO PROVIDE FOR THE AMENDMENT IN CANADA OF THE CONSTITUTION OF CANADA

speechtext:
Whereas the Parliament of Canada and the legislatures of each and every province of Canada have requested, and consented to, the enactment of an act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom in the terms hereinafter set forth, and the Senate and House of Commons of Canada in Parliament assembled have submitted addresses to Her Majesty praying that Her Majesty may graciously be pleased to cause a bill to be laid before the Parliament of the United Kingdom for that purpose:
Be it therefore enacted by the Queen's most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, in this present Parliament assembled, and by the authority of the same, as follows:

maintopic: POWER TO AMEND THE CONSTITUTION OF CANADA

speechtext:
1.	Subject to this part, the Parliament of Canada may make laws repealing, amending or re-enacting any provision of the Constitution of Canada.
2.	No law made under the authority of this part affecting any provision of this act or section 51A of the British North America Act, 1867, or affecting any provision of the Constitution of Canada relating to
(а)	the powers of the legislature of a province to make laws,
(б)	the rights or privileges granted or secured by the Constitution of Canada to the legislature or the government of a province,
(c)	the assets or property of a province, or
(d)	the use of the English or French language,
shall come into force unless it is concurred in by the legislatures of all the provinces.
3.	(1) No law made under the authority of this part affecting any provision of the Constitution of Canada that refers to one or more, but not all, of the provinces, shall come into force unless it is concurred in by the legislature of every province to which the provision refers.
(2) Section 2 of this act does not extend to any provision of the Constitution of Canada referred to in subsection (I) of this section.
4.	(1) No law made under the authority of this part affecting any provision of the Constitution of Canada relating to education in any province other than Newfoundland shall come into force unless it is concurred in by the legislatures of all the provinces other than Newfoundland.
(2)	No law made under the authority of this part affecting any provision of the Constitution of Canada relating to education in the province of Newfoundland shall come into force unless it is concurred in by the legislature of the province of Newfoundland.
(3)	Sections 2 and 3 of this act do not extend to any provision of the Constitution of Canada referred to in subsection (1) or (2) of this section.
5.	No law made under the authority of this part affecting any provision of the Constitution of Canada, not coming within sections 2, 3 or 4 of this act, shall come into force if such law is rejected by any combination of provincial Legislatures representative of not less than 20 per cent of the population of Canada (according to the latest census) within a period of 24 months after its passage by the Parliament of Canada.
6.	Notwithstanding anything in the Constitution of Canada, the Parliament of Canada may exclusively make laws from time to time amending the Constitution of Canada in relation to the executive Government of Canada, and the Senate and House of Commons, except as regards
(a)	the functions of the Queen and the Governor General in relation to the Parliament or Government of Canada;
(b)	the requirements of the Constitution of Canada respecting a yearly session of Parliament;

He said: Mr. Speaker, every member in this House has been humbled today by the passage of a motion stating that the Parliament of Canada submit an address to Her Majesty, Queen Elizabeth, that Her Majesty may graciously be pleased to cause a bill to be laid before the Parliament of the United Kingdom to provide for the amendment in Canada of the Constitution of Canada.
Parliament must pursue this objective with haste. This is the beginning of a dream that so many of us have cherished for so long; a dream to make this nation whole, to give this nation a distinctiveness, a wholesomeness, a Canadianism that is our own, and sovereignty as a nation and as a people.
Let us hope and let us pray that this process which has begun here today will not falter and fail. Let us all be determined that we shall succeed in patriating our constitution with provincial unanimous agreements, but without, if necessary, for the Parliament of Canada can patriate the constitution with a built-in formula of unanimity for the subsequent amendment of the Constitution in Canada. The question is, has Parliament got the will to do it?
Let us also be determined that we shall succeed in adopting a less rigid formula for amendment so that we can preserve what is good in our constitution and yet change with some ease what needs changing to keep pace with the evolution of the Canadian identity and the Canadian reality.
Let us also be determined to stay united as a nation and as a people so that we can live in peace, in harmony, in prosperity, and in mutual respect of each other's cultures, each other's languages, and the rights and responsibilities of each and every one of us.
The history of our search as Canadians for identity, for distinctiveness and for fulfilment, has been long and sometimes filled with divisiveness, yet always there has been a common

May 9, 1980
Constitutional Amendment
bond between us, for we were and we still are the children of adventurers, the sons and daughters of pioneers who laboured fiercely to give us a future, a future of opportunity and freedom beyond comparison with any other country in the history of civilization.
I plead with the people of Quebec not to cast themselves adrift from this most magnificent of human organizations where opportunity can and should be on the basis of equality for all, where humanism can be respected as the highest order of human organization. This House must act to follow up this motion. A properly structured address to the Queen must evolve. A meeting of first ministers must be convened to get agreement from the premiers. As I have said before, the first ministers should not only attend that conference some time in the near future, but the leaders of the opposition parties in each and every province, and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) in this House as well.
The reason I say that is because on this fundamental matter, the most basic law of this country, leaders of the opposition in some of the provinces indeed represent a greater percentage of the people in their province than the premiers. Indeed, in this House it is perfectly obvious that the one national force we have from coast to coast is the Progressive Conservative Party. The Leader of the Opposition in this House should be a full participant in that constitutional conference which will be convened in the next several months.
If agreement is not unanimous among the provinces after the conference of the first ministers and the leaders of the opposition, then the Parliament of Canada can act as it is obligated to act and should act to patriate the constitution with the built-in formula in the BNA Act, that is, unanimous agreement between the provinces and the federal government for any subsequent change to the constitution, the only change being that it will now be done in Canada.
It is well-known, and has been stated on several occasions by the Parliament of the United Kingdom, that if the Parliament of Canada approached the Parliament of the United Kingdom and the Queen, the Parliament of the United Kingdom would follow the dictates and the request or the submissions made by this Parliament to patriate the Canadian Constitution and make it an act of Canada.
There is a substantive history on the attempts to patriate the constitution and find an amending formula. It has been a history of failure, of smallness and of inadequacy on the part of politicians. It was during the federal-provincial conference of 1927 that questions concerning the constitution and its amendment were first debated. The search for an actual amending formula was reinitiated and addressed under the leadership of the late prime minister, the Hon. John Diefen-baker, in the 1960s. Debates emerging from that period centred on the search for a constitutional amending formula and resulted in the Fulton-Favreau formula of 1964.
At the conclusion of the federal-provincial conference held in Charlottetown on September 1 and 2, 1964, to commemorate the centennial of the conference of the Fathers of Confederation which took place in that city in 1864, the then prime minister, the late Hon. Lester B. Pearson, and the premiers issued a communique. In it the late prime minister and the premiers affirmed their unanimous decision to conclude the patriation of the BNA Act without delay.
The communique added that they decided to complete the procedure for amending the constitution of Canada based on the draft legislation proposed at the constitutional conference of 1961, which they accepted in principle. The attorneys general of Canada then met to complete the formula. At a conference of Canadian first ministers on October 14, 1964, the first ministers unanimously agreed on an amending formula. The communique issued by the late prime minister Pearson and the premiers from the conference states that when the amending procedures become law, all future amendments to Canada's constitution will be made in Canada instead of by the Parliament of the United Kingdom. The communique added the following:
As a result our constitution will have become, for the first time in the history of Canada, truly and wholly Canadian.
This occurred back in 1964 under the guidance of the Prime Minister of Canada at that time, who was the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson.
The bill contained within this motion contains an attempt to find an amending formula, a structured, multistaged amending formula. I had a similar resolution on an order paper of the Thirty-first Parliament which was well debated by myself, the now Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Guigan), the NDP member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Miss Jewett) and the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). That debate is well documented in Hansard of October 22, 1979.
Again, 1 would like to summarize very quickly the basic principles of this motion which contains a bill to patriate the constitution with an amending formula. The principles are as follows: The BNA Act of 1867 served this nation well and renewal should be gradual and step-wise. The whole logistic approach of evolving a whole new constitution has proven to be unsuccessful. The package is so large that politicians and the Canadian people find it hard to swallow in one lump. It is a lump created in the throat and we choke on it and we fail.
I am suggesting in this motion that the step-wise approach is the more appropriate approach. The second principle in this motion is that this bill would effectively patriate the constitution of Canada and provide a formula for subsequent revision in Canada. The bill incorporates a constitutional-amending formula which has in it at least five very distinctive and important parts. First, it requires the unanimous agreement of the provinces to amend certain provincial powers including natural resource ownership and the use of the French language and the English language.
The second part is that it generally permits the provinces to amend their own provincial constitutions and, thirdly, it generally permits the federal government to amend the constitution on purely federal matters only. Fourth, it provides the people
May 9, 1980

of Canada with a mechanism for amending their own constitution. In my history, in government and in politics, which now spans over a decade, I have always been unimpressed with the fact that politicians seem to think that they have the only God-given right to change the basic laws of this country.
I want to suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that when it comes to the very basic laws of this country, it is not only the politicians who have a right to change those basic laws, but like most other countries-for example, the United States-and federations, of which Canada is the third oldest, the people have the right to initiate a constitutional change. They have the right, for example, to tell their elected politicians that in certain instances they need a very basic change to human rights and to certain matters of the constitution which affect people in every walk of life.
Nevertheless, one must have the safeguards. If one looks at this bill one finds that it is full of safeguards to protect people's actions to change their own basic law. It says that it must start with a plebiscite or a petition, followed by a referendum, and that referendum must pass in each and every province to the extent of at least 50 per cent of the voting population; and furthermore, that the amendment should receive at least a 75 per cent plurality on a total basis. This amending formula provides a formula for amending the constitution generally in all other areas.
I want to speak on this matter for just a few minutes, Mr. Speaker. 1 know 1 can speak for at least an hour on this subject but I do not have too much time, and anyway you would not allow it.
What I want to speak about is the formula for changing the constitution in all other areas besides those I have indicated. We have had the Victoria Charter which said that Quebec shall have, in perpetuity, a veto; it said that Ontario shall have, in perpetuity, a veto; that two out of the four Atlantic provinces shall have a veto, and two out of the four western provinces, provided they have 50 per cent of the population of those four provinces shall have a veto-in perpetuity, all of them, until it is changed again.
This country is changing, Mr. Speaker. The population is shifting, and although one might set a constitution at any moment in time on a basis of population in Ontario, there is absolutely nothing to guarantee that that population and that percentage of the population in Ontario will exist 50 years hence. If a fixed formula in terms of veto power is provided for the province of Ontario, the province of Quebec or any province, in perpetuity, then how can it be changed? How can it be changed, regardless of what the population becomes 50 or 100 years hence? Constitutions are the basic law of the nation and this should apply equally to all parts of the nation. If the population of Newfoundland went up to 10 per cent, 15 per cent or 20 per cent of the population of Canada, would it not also then need a veto? Or British Columbia if the same thing happened there?
Constitutional Amendment
What I have suggested is that any combination of provinces across the nation, from the east to the west, from the centre to the outlying areas, any combination of provinces representing a minimum of 20 per cent of the population of Canada, should have a veto.
This type of formula is a futuristic one, Mr. Speaker, as well a formula for the present, so that if the population shifts, the formula shifts so that the little province can combine with the big province to get a veto; so that the Atlantic province which has an interest in offshore resources can combine with the province of British Columbia which has an interest in offshore resources, to say no-no way can central Canada take our resources from us for the good of central Canada, because the initial constitution provided those resources primarily for the growth and benefit of a region.
There is a certain degree of equalization in this nation and it is necessary, vitally necessary, but we can get into a process of over-equalization. Indeed, we are now in a process of overequalization in this nation, such that the regions are stifled, such that the process of co-operation between the regions is increasingly under stress and strain. We have a country now that is moving toward falling apart because we do not respect the very basis of that constitution in the first place, and that is that the resources which come under section 109 of the British North America Act of each and every province should not be taxed by either one jurisdiction or by the Government of Canada.
But what does the government do? It taxes the resources of one province in interprovincial trade; it taxes the resources of one province in international trade. That is totally inappropriate under section 109 of the British North America Act, the existing constitution. It does not tax gold, it does not tax nickel, it does not tax asbestos, it does not tax hydropower and it does not tax all the other resources. I can tell you that 70 per cent of the world's nickel was sold by Ontario not so many years ago. The proceeds of the sale, in terms of total mineral wealth, was very high. I can also tell you, Mr. Speaker, that oil and gas now represent some Sll billion out of $22 billion annual mineral wealth in the nation and that the actual flow westward literally is only another $5 billion a year which, on the basis of the gross national product of this nation, is not high. It is just a few percentage points.
What is wrong with capital flowing west or east in such a way that the development of this nation is regional in scope and so that our young people can move from one end of the country to the other and find great opportunities everywhere? At the same time, that formula for the well-being and for opportunities for young Canadians from one end of the country to the other, can be maintained in such a way that our cultures and our languages can be preserved.
That is the future dream of this country-a future dream which says that people will not stay fixed in one area because they get handouts, when at the same time there are great opportunities in other areas of the country. That is the future dream of this country-a new constitution that will provide this entire nation with the dreams and aspirations and the

May 9, 1980
Constitutional Amendment
future well-being of young Canadians. Young Canadians should enjoy this nation from one end to the other; young Quebeckers should enjoy this nation from one end to the other without giving up their culture, their language, their history, their roots, their traditions and their emotions. This can be done, Mr. Speaker. We can make out of this nation the most magnificent nation in all of civilization if we put our minds to it.
One of the things that makes my blood boil is the narrow politician, the politician with the narrowest perspective that one can imagine. That is what I have seen across this nation as the president of the Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers, for example, in all the meetings I have had with ministers from all over this nation and, indeed, in meetings outside this country. With some latitude and some depth of thinking we can, in fact, make this a great country, Mr. Speaker, and 1 hope we do.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Kenneth Robinson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) for his very eloquent presentation. He is probably one of those in this House who is most knowledgeable on the subject. In fact he presented the same motion in October, 1979, at which time he spoke with great eloquence as well.
It is also timely that this morning the hon. member presented a motion under Standing Order 43 concerning the patria-tion of our constitution, and now he has presented a motion for the amendment in Canada of the Constitution of Canada.
It is important that all the provinces and the federal government agree on this, so the hon. member's motion is very timely. He knows how difficult it has been in the past to change our constitution or, in fact, to patriate it. Many attempts have been made to patriate the constitution and I want to put some of those on the record in order to show how difficult it is to partriate the constitution, or even to change it.
The publication of the Balfour report in 1926 opened the door for Canada to remove itself completely from the legislative authority of the British parliament. The principal problem to be resolved was that of finding an amending formula for the British North America Act when patriated. That, of course, is what we are talking about today-the whole question of finding a magic formula that is going to patriate the constitution and allow Canada to change its constitution in Canada.
The first attempt to solve the problem occurred in 1927 at a dominion-provincial conference. That conference examined an opinion submitted by the then minister of justice, Ernest Lapointe, which involved patriation with a special amending formula. The agreement of all participants was not forthcoming and the matter was kept under consideration.
A second attempt to resolve this matter of patriation was at the dominion-provincial conference held in April, 1931, which was convened in response to representations by Ontario. Once
again they were unable to reach any conclusion and the matter was held over once again for subsequent consideration and approval.
The third attempt to deal with the matter occurred in January, 1935, when the House of Commons established a special committee to inquire into the need to amend the British North America Act and a procedure for amendment. Apparently the committee held some ten sessions but did not propose a procedure for amendment in that report. It is strange that a committee of the House of Commons itself could not come up with any formula acceptable at that time, and apparently we are still in the same situation today.
The fourth attempt originated in the dominion-provincial conference of 1935 which established a subconference on constitutional questions under the chairmanship of the minister of justice, Ernest Lapointe. Following a recommendation of the subconference, a continuing committee on constitutional questions was convened on January 28, 1936. The committee devised an amending formula incorporating elements of flexibility and entrenchment, but once again it was not adopted. And so it goes on and on.
The fifth attempt to deal with the matter was limited to the question of the power of the federal Parliament to amend the constitution of Canada, except for five protected categories, the current situation with respect to constitutional amendment that we have. The federal Parliament unilaterally requested that the British Parliament pass the British North America Act, 1949, which would grant this power to the Parliament of Canada under the new section. This in effect did happen. But that only happened with regard to Newfoundland entering into confederation with the rest of Canada.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: And with the agreement of Newfoundland.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
Exactly, with the agreement of Newfoundland.
The sixth attempt occurred in 1950 when a constitutional conference was convened in Ottawa in January and continued its work in Quebec City in September. It was subsequently suspended because of the Korean crisis and the work was not resumed.
The seventh attempt was in July, 1960, at the dominion-provincial conference in Ottawa. The conference of attorneys general met four times during the succeeding 14 months and could reach no conclusion. At first the minister of justice, Mr. E. D. Fulton, suggested that the authority to amend the constitution of Canada in all respects, not known amendable in Canada, be transferred to the Parliament of Canada, subject to the consent of the legislatures of all the provinces. It was generally felt, however, that a less rigid formula could be found. A formula was devised in November, 1961, but some differences of view remained and the plan was not carried through. Of course, we are all aware of the Favreau formula which has not yet been adopted.
May 9, 1980

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The Fulton-Favreau formula.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
An eighth attempt began at the suggestion of Prime Minister Pearson in 1964. This was mentioned by the hon. member for Edmonton East previously. At that time nothing further transpired. At a federal-provincial conference held in October of the same year, a modified version of the 1961 proposal was approved in principle, but subsequently it failed to get unanimous support, and consideration was postponed indefinitely. That is what usually happens every time there is a conference on the constitution.
The ninth attempt began with the federal-provincial conference of February, 1968, which became a continuing constitutional conference. The constitutional conference with its various committees of ministers and officials and its subcommittees and so on operated from 1968 until the Victoria charter, in Victoria, in June, 1971. The charter provided for a patriation procedure, an amending formula, to which all governments there represented agreed, and a number of changes in substantive areas, as well as for the modernization of the constitution. Quebec, however, has not prepared to proceed with the full charter, and once again action was suspended. 1 think the Victoria amending formula itself is very important to orchestrate at this time. The amending formula as approved, basically provided that the legislative assembly of a province or either the Senate or the House of Commons could initiate a resolution for amendment of the constitution. If the amendment applied to one or more, but not all of the provinces, it might be made when authorized by resolutions of the Senate and the House of Commons and the legislative assembly of each of the provinces concerned.
For other amendments, the amendment would have to be authorized by resolutions of the Senate and the House of Commons and by the legislative assemblies of a majority of the provinces including: first, any province that had, at any time prior to the proclamation according to any previous general census, a population of at least 25 per cent of the population of Canada-and that is where this differs somewhat from that proposed by the hon. member for Edmonton East, since he is talking about 20 per cent of the population; second, of at least two of the Atlantic provinces; third, of at least two of the western provinces that have, according to the then latest general census, combined populations of at least 50 per cent of the population of all the western provinces. I assume when we are talking about the western provinces that we are really talking about Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
If the Senate, under either formula, did not pass a resolution within 90 days of a resolution being passed by the House of Commons, the House of Commons could pass the resolution again after the expiry of 90 days and thus authorize the Governor General on behalf of the Parliament of Canada to issue a proclamation.
The amending formula had been approved at the Victoria conference without the dissent of any province. It was because
Constitutional Amendment
of that general agreement that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) hoped it could be reaffirmed and made the basis of early agreement on patriation.
On the occasion of the discussion in April, 1975, the Premier of Quebec indicated that his province could not agree to patriation on the basis proposed without cultural guarantees. In the course of subsequent discussions, other first ministers suggested further additions to patriation plus the amending formula. These included the parts of the Victoria charter concerning the Supreme Court and regional disparities. Some western first ministers queried the population qualification in the amending formula for western provinces. However, no such qualification applies to the Atlantic provinces.
If all provincial governments agree to the amending formula, with or without the population qualification for the western provinces, to appropriate cultural guarantees, to the provisions respecting the Supreme Court and to the provisions respecting regional disparities, one could proceed toward patriation according to the procedure outlined in February, 1971. This is the solution that is proposed by the federal government.
Now the matter has been of continuing concern to the previous Liberal governments from time to time over a period of years, as a matter of fact, for some ten years from 1968 to 1978. I recall that in 1975 the Prime Minister of Canada invited two provincial premiers to take part in a further attempt to bring control over the British North America Act from Great Britain to Canada and to agree on a new system for amending the act once it was brought home. At that time, once again, although the former leader of the opposition, the Hon. Robert Stanfield, agreed and felt, as he stated at that time, that he did not think it was too much to ask that there be agreement at least on an amendment formula during the life of the Parliament, of course, as we all know, nothing transpired further as a result of this attempt either.
However, in 1979, during the election campaign the hon. member for Mount Royal, on May 10 in Montreal stated;
If you elect us, if you give us your support, if we form the government after the next election, we will have a Liberal government that will set in motion the patriation of the constitution.
That is all the more reason why it is so important today that this matter is before the House of Commons once again. I think it is fitting also that this matter was brought in by a member of the opposition to indicate that there is continued interest on both sides of the House to patriate our constitution. The Prime Minister went on to say:
It will be a Liberal government that will do this. We will do it with the co-operation of the provinces, if possible. And if that co-operation is not forthcoming, we will do it with the co-operation of the Canadian people, by means of a referendum.
What he has really illustrated here is not too different from what was suggested by the hon. member for Edmonton East in that it may be necessary to have a referendum on this kind of matter in order to let the people of Canada decide for themselves if in fact they wish to patriate the constitution.

May 9, 1980
Constitutional Amendment
1 would suggest that some form of referendum might also be considered when we are looking toward changes in the constitution as well in so far as it affects all of Canada and not just individual provinces.
As the Prime Minister said this morning, with regard to the motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43, that, if possible, we want to deal with the provinces. The House leader for the opposition orchestrated the same thing: we do want to work with the provinces. This is an important matter, particularly since the powers of the provinces and the federal government fall under sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act. The provision is that there should be agreement if possible to reach any conclusions with regard to changes in our constitutional or patriation of the constitution itself.
If all this negotiation fails, it would seem to me that in due course some action would have to be taken, possibly through a referendum, and as 1 mentioned before, this has already been suggested by the hon. member for Edmonton East. When 1 look at this bill, and I do not want to go into it in detail, I see that it provides for amendments and not patriation. It is unfortunate the hon. member did not feel he should bring patriation into it at the same time. If we have an amendment to the British North America Act, we want to have the power to make it here and not through the British Parliament.
Clause 1 is very important as it states the power will be in the Parliament of Canada to make laws, repealing, amending, or re-enacting any provisions of the constitution of Canada. That is a very far-reaching and wide power. It would probably require a great deal of discussion and debate before we could reach a conclusion on it.
As far as clause 2 is concerned, all provinces must agree on changes affecting the provinces. There is no doubt that this is well taken. I am sure there would be agreement on all sides that the provinces should be able to have a veto vote if it affects them directly. By the same token, they should be able to effect changes in the constitution if they are affected themselves, even though other provinces may not agree. This could be controversial. I cannot think of any possible problem at the present time that would make it desirable for one province not to agree with another province. However, that remains to be seen.
Clause 5 speaks of 20 per cent of the population rejecting a vote. It seems that this is a very small percentage and it should not be too difficult to obtain.
Don't talk it out.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
I really have not got much more to say. I want to say something with regard to clause 12 which talks about the right of self-determination. It is what you might call a selective right to determination only for people who are of either of the two linguistic groups, which he calls solitudes, French and English. This is something that might be considered unsupportable. It would have to be considered very carefully. Even if it were orchestrated by a referendum, I doubt whether it would carry.
When you look at clause 12, you must also look at clause 7(2) where the hon. member suggests that no province or even a part of a province could secede.
In summary, this is a very timely matter to be brought before the House of Commons. It is a matter we will be hearing much more of again. I am sorry there is not a longer debate so that more members could have the opportunity to say what they have to say about this very important matter. I again thank the hon. member for bringing it before the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, 1 begin by saying that today we are talking about something that is very important. It has been and will be with us for a long period of time. The first note I want to strike is one of caution which I do not think was really in the speech made by the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko). In my opinion, it is very important that we not bring back the constitution to this country without the unanimous consent of all the provinces. That is very important.
It is also important that Parliament not pass any resolution or bill outlining the details of what we want to see as a Parliament without there first being negotiations between all the provinces and the federal Parliament of this country. I see some Conservatives nodding their heads in agreement. I am pleased to see that. Before we do something that fundamental, we must first have negotiations between the provinces and the federal Parliament and come up with something on which we all agree. That is the reason why I cannot support the resolution before us today.
The hon. member for Edmonton East asks, does Parliament have the will? I am sure that Parliament has the will to see a reconstituted constitution in Canada. However, I again underline the important part, that we only want to do that if we bring all the provinces with us. One of the basic laws of a federation is that all parts of that federation are treated as equals and all parts of that federation must meet together, plan together and agree on things together as one family. If we do not do that, there will be very serious problems within that federation.
There is another point, minor, and perhaps I should not mention it. The hon. member for Edmonton East, and it is typical of some of the oversights, said that at constitutional conferences all the first ministers should be there and leaders of the opposition. I say to him in passing that that does not include representatives of all the people. If we have conferences of the Parliaments and the legislatures, it should not only be of the two parties. I remind him that in this House, for example, his party represents 33 per cent of the people. Our party represents nearly 20 per cent of the people. Therefore, if there is any conference of any kind that involves more than just first ministers, it should reflect the legislative will of all the peoples.
May 9, 1980

That is why it is important to think of the province of Quebec as well. I cannot predict whether the Oui or Non votes will win. Regardless of who wins in the province of Quebec, there will be a large bloc of people not on the winning side and they must be represented in any conference held on the constitution of this country.
There are a number of things in terms of specifics that really concern me about the resolution before the House. The hon. member kept referring to it as a bill.
It is a bill within a resolution.

Perhaps that is what it is. It might be bootlegging. In clause 2 he talks about those things that cannot be done without agreement of all the provinces. He talks about the power the provinces have already, the assets of a province and so on. In subclause (d) he talks about the use of the English or French language. You go to clause 6(h) and he again talks about the use of the English and French language, that nothing can be done there without the agreement of all the provinces. I differ strongly with him on this. His leader, the former prime minister, differs strongly with him as well.
This Parliament and all parties in it passed an Official Languages Act which states that the federal government has the right to enact legislation on the official languages of this country. What the hon. member is trying to do here is render Parliament into what could be called a parliamentary unit where it would not have any power or authority over legislation when it comes to vfficial languages in our institutions. Therefore I can never support a bill on that account.
All you have to do is go back to what has already been agreed upon by the premiers. I go back to the Victoria charter, article 18, page 88, where it says that the federal Parliament has the right to enact legislation regarding the French and English languages in our institutions. I can also look at the special joint committee on the constitution in 1972 which said that we have that right. At the premiers' conference in 1978 the premiers agreed unanimously that we have that power. The government's bill, brought in by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in 1978, two years ago, also said we have that right. In this resolution there is a suggestion that clearly goes against the expressed wishes of the provinces, the people's representatives and groups that have studied the issue.
As I said at the beginning, the fundamental matter of importance here is that there be co-operation, agreement and consultation between all the provinces of this country and the federal Parliament.
The second thing which concerns me is section 6 of the proposed act, and here the hon. member is talking about the resolution, or the bill, as he calls it. It says:
Notwithstanding anything in the Constitution of Canada, the Parliament of Canada may exclusively make laws from time to time amending the Constitution of Canada in relation to the executive Government of Canada, and the Senate and House of Commons-
Constitutional Amendment
I disagree with this too. 1 think we can make laws pertaining to the House of Commons and perhaps the executive of the Government of Canada, but I disagree when it comes to the Senate. I am not referring here just to the position taken by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that the Senate should be abolished. I think that is a correct position.
Midnight tonight.

I refer also to Claude Ryan's paper and the Pepin-Robarts task force. I refer to positions now being talked about by various provinces, including my own, the province of Saskatchewan, whereby the Senate should be abolished and perhaps replaced by some other institution. Such an institution might perhaps be a council of the provinces. The provinces would appoint or elect people to represent directly the provinces here in the Senate. I am not sure exactly what this organization should be; all I am saying is that when it comes to the Senate and the future of the Senate, the provinces should have some say. We should not have the unilateral say when it comes to the Senate, and for that reason too I cannot support the resolution before the House today.
The hon. member lists all kinds of things which are exceptions, and amongst them is not the Supreme Court of Canada. When we get to the Supreme Court, we are getting to something which is very dear to the hearts of the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), myself and Quebeckers. I think now of the question of asbestos and so forth. I am talking about resources. The Supreme Court is appointed by the federal government, and we in Saskatchewan have some problems with rulings made by the Supreme Court when it comes to oil-the CIGOL case-and when it comes to potash. Now the Quebec government is having similar problems with the courts when it comes to asbestos.
We feel that the province has the right to tax resources or to nationalize potash, asbestos or what have you. Those matters are under provincial law. The Supreme Court has been taking differing positions on some of these issues, and I think perhaps one reason it does so is that the judges are appointed by the federal government. What we are saying, and what many provinces are saying, is that some of those judges should be appointed by the provinces because those judges have to adjudicate and make rulings on conflicts between the provinces and the federal government, and they should therefore be appointed, some by the federal government and some by the provinces. Otherwise there perhaps could be a bit of a conflict of interest. In his resolution the hon. member leaves this to the exclusive power of the federal government. I do not think the premier of Alberta would agree with that being in the resolution here today. I do not think he would agree at all.
Another thing the hon. member talks about here is the right of the provinces to secede from the union. He says that before any province can secede, an act of Parliament must be passed and acts in each of the legislatures must be passed. I will not try to speculate on what the solution should be, but again that is something which had to be negotiated amongst all the

May 9, 1980
Constitutional Amendment
people of this country. I think, for example, of Newfoundland. Newfoundland came into this country as a result of a vote in Newfoundland, an act of the Newfoundland assembly and by an act of this Parliament. An act did not have to go through the legislatures of Saskatchewan, New Brunswick and all the other provinces of this country.
As 1 keep going along here in this resolution I come to No. 10. The hon. member talks about referendums, and he says that if the people of Canada petition, they can have a referendum on any constitutional matter, and if 5 per cent or more of the people petition for such, there can be a referendum on any constitutional matter. What is a constitutional matter? Here we are getting into a very sensitive thing. We are getting into constitutional matters which pertain to the federal government, to the provinces and to the territories. In constitutional matters there are concurrent powers.
Then the hon. member goes on to say that if 75 per cent of the people agree in a national plebiscite and 50 per cent of the people in each of the provinces agree, the federal government must then enact the law or the wish expressed in the referendum. I think this too is very dangerous in a federation because, for example, it might be easy to get that vote across Canada when it comes to authority over oil. The rest of the country may say, by 80 per cent, that perhaps Alberta has a little bit too much power. It might be a very divisive issue in Alberta, but it may pass because of the wording of the referendum question by, say, 51 per cent to 49 per cent. There might be immense division, but the federal government would then have the obligation to make the intent of that resolution the law of this country. I just do not think that that is the type of thing we should have in a resolution or in a law of this Parliament. I think that again is an infringement on the rights of the provinces.
There is another thing which I find very interesting, and that is the proposed section 12. The way it is worded in English and French is contradictory. In English it says:
-the Constitution of Canada as revised, this act recognizes that Canada is a multicultural nation composed primarily of two linguistic solitudes, namely English and French.
In the French version it says:
Cette loi reconnait que le Canada est une nation multiculturelle composee cssentiellement de deux groupes linguistiques, a savoir I'anglais et le fransais.
The hon. member is talking about two different groups, but in English he is talking about two solitudes. I think that is getting rather dangerous. I looked up the definitions of "solitude" and "solitary" in the Oxford dictionary, and I found out that "solitary" means living alone, without companions, secluded, single, lonely, sole, by yourself, and I just maintain that that is not the situation in Canada today. We have in this country peoples in two linguistic groups, but there is a tremendous amount of interaction between those peoples.
[ Translation]
We are all in the same Parliament. We can speak either French or English.

Francophone members can, Anglophone members can and other people can. We have a tremendous interaction amongst the peoples. If there were two solitudes, in the first place why talk about the separation of the solitudes, because they are already separated? How can a solitude seek separation? I just do not understand how we can spend time talking about the integrity of Canada if this country is already being divided, as the hon. member implies, in the two solitudes. I just cannot buy that type of philosophy which is in the resolution before us today.

Another very important thing in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, is that paragraph 12 totally contradicts the principle of selfdetermination for Quebeckers. The New Democratic Party has always recognized the rights of Quebeckers to choose freely and without coercion their political future.
It is the first time, Mr. Speaker, that such an argument is put in the House, and I refer specifically to this sentence in paragraph 12.

It says here:
Furthermore, that such separation, if and when decided upon by the solitude seeking separation-
This could be either the English or French solitude.
-shall occur not along established provincial territorial boundaries but along such contiguous territorial boundaries that are duly and legally negotiated between the two solitudes but which fully respect the rights of large minorities and their expressed option to remain with the solitude of their choice.
I wonder if anybody can explain to me what all this fuddly, muddly gobbledygook really means. It only says that either solitude can, and I quote:
-secede each from the other if so desired and duly and legally expressed through a referendum supported in a near unanimous fashion by the people of the solitude seeking separation.
That means you can secede by a near unanimous fashion. What is a near unanimous fashion? What is a near unanimous vote?
I put that question because again there is no elaboration in the resolution before us on what the hon. member sees as a near unanimous vote.
Those are only a few of the things one could refer to in the resolution which I think do not make much sense at all.
Mr. Speaker, I see that you are telling me to wind up, so I suggest that the best thing to do with the resolution before the House today is to send it down to the paper shredder so that it can be shredded and thrown into the garbag; can. I think all the people of this country, including PT.mier Lougheed, would be very happy with that accomplishment.
